153: With the rapid development of fields such as marine resource exploitation, marine environmental monitoring and underwater engineering inspection, underwater vision technology has gradually become an important means of acquiring marine information. With the release of the New Generation Artificial Intelligence Development Plan, an explicit requirement was set for China to become the world's principal AI innovation centre by 2030, and this includes key technical fields such as deep learning and image processing. Against this backdrop, underwater vision technology has become a core means of acquiring marine information. Among these, the acquisition of high-quality underwater images is the prerequisite for achieving accurate object detection. By raising the resolution and level of detail of underwater images through super-resolution reconstruction technology, and then combining this with object detection methods, precise perception for biological identification, target localisation and resource surveying can be achieved in systems such as underwater robots, autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) and remotely operated vehicles (ROVs), providing reliable technical support for underwater scientific research and engineering.
154: The underwater imaging environment is complex, and light propagation is simultaneously affected by absorption and scattering. The absorption effect causes light of different wavelengths to attenuate at different rates; among them, blue light attenuates relatively slowly, causing images to exhibit a blue-green colour cast. The scattering effect deflects light from its original path: forward scattering blurs edge details, while backward scattering reduces contrast and sharpness. As a result, underwater images generally suffer from low contrast, colour distortion, blurred details and noise interference, which makes it difficult for traditional vision algorithms to accurately extract target features and limits the performance of detection systems, as shown in Figure 1.1. To cope with the complex interference of the underwater imaging environment, many scholars have taken a hardware approach and designed high-precision, high-speed cameras to improve image acquisition quality. Although such equipment reduces noise to a certain extent and mitigates the influence of the water body on imaging, the acquired images still lack fine detail and texture information and struggle to meet the requirements of subsequent object detection or analysis tasks; at the same time they are expensive, which is unfavourable for large-scale application. By contrast, underwater image super-resolution reconstruction technology can, without changing the original imaging equipment, restore details and textures lost in low-resolution images. This not only significantly improves image quality but also provides richer feature information for object detection, achieving effective coupling between image enhancement and target recognition, and thereby improving the accuracy and stability of underwater target localisation and recognition. As shown in Figure 1.2, processed underwater images can substantially increase the number of matched feature points.

160: In summary, this thesis proposes a complete underwater visual perception framework whose main thread is "original underwater image -> super-resolution sharpening -> high-quality clear image -> object detection -> detection result". This framework organically links the two modules of image quality improvement and object detection: first, a deep-learning-based super-resolution reconstruction method is used to enhance the originally degraded image, restoring its texture details, improving colour imbalance and raising contrast; then, with the high-quality clear image as input, an improved object detection model performs precise recognition and localisation of underwater targets. Experimental research shows that performing object detection after enhancement processing of underwater images can effectively improve the model's detection accuracy, thereby improving overall detection performance. Therefore, researching deep-learning-based underwater image super-resolution reconstruction and object detection methods has important theoretical significance and application value for improving the performance of underwater vision systems.
161: 1.2 Research Status at Home and Abroad
162: 1.2.1 Research Status of Underwater Image Super-Resolution Reconstruction
163: Image super-resolution (SR) reconstruction technology aims to recover high-resolution (HR) image detail from low-resolution (LR) images, and has important application value in fields such as medical imaging, remote sensing and underwater vision. With the rise of deep learning, super-resolution methods based on convolutional neural networks have achieved substantive breakthroughs. SRCNN, proposed by Dong et al., was the first to introduce convolutional neural networks into the field of image super-resolution;
165: through a three-layer convolutional structure it learns an end-to-end mapping from low-resolution to high-resolution images, establishing the foundational
166: paradigm of deep learning super-resolution research [1]. VDSR, proposed by Kim et al., introduced global residual learning and used an extremely deep network structure to improve reconstruction accuracy [2]. Lim et al. designed the enhanced deep residual network EDSR, removing batch-normalisation layers and expanding network capacity, substantially improving performance on general super-resolution benchmarks [3]. RDN, proposed by Zhang et al., makes full use of hierarchical features through residual dense connections, achieving comprehensive recovery of multi-scale detail [4]; Zhang et al. further introduced a channel attention mechanism to propose RCAN, which adaptively weights the feature responses of different channels so that the network can selectively focus on the key information required for high-frequency reconstruction [5]. In terms of generative adversarial network applications, the GAN framework proposed by Goodfellow et al. provided a new avenue for improving super-resolution image quality [6]; SRGAN, proposed by Ledig et al., was the first to introduce GANs into image super-resolution reconstruction, introducing a perceptual loss function to drive the network to generate high-frequency visual detail [7]; building on this, Wang et al. proposed ESRGAN, which further enhanced the realism of texture reconstruction through residual dense blocks and a relativistic GAN loss, becoming an important benchmark for subsequent research [8]. Zhao Ran et al. proposed a medical ultrasound image super-resolution reconstruction method based on video multi-frame fusion, effectively improving reconstruction resolution through cross-frame integration of temporal information [9]; Ran Wenbing et al. combined generative adversarial networks with attention mechanisms, significantly improving the super-resolution reconstruction of medical images [10]. In the remote-sensing image field, Zhao Huiyan et al. proposed a GAN-based super-resolution analysis method for Sentinel-2 remote-sensing images [11]; Zhang Yan et al. proposed a high-resolution satellite image reconstruction scheme based on an HMRF prior model, improving the structural fidelity of reconstruction results by introducing Markov random field constraints [12]. The body of methods formed by the above work provides important reference for the underwater image super-resolution research of this thesis. In research on underwater image quality improvement, early work relied mainly on physical imaging models for image restoration. Yang Aiping et al. proposed an underwater image restoration method based on colour-distortion removal and the dark channel prior, improving colour reproduction by estimating underwater light attenuation parameters [13]; Yang Aiping et al. further proposed a single-image underwater sharpening method based on multi-feature fusion, comprehensively exploiting colour, structural and texture features to achieve image enhancement - however, these methods lack robustness in scenes where water quality conditions are complex and highly variable [14]. Addressing the particular nature of underwater image degradation, researchers began to design specialised super-resolution methods for underwater scenes. Islam et al. constructed the USR-248 underwater image super-resolution dataset and proposed the SRDRM method, effectively restoring texture detail in underwater images through multi-scale residual learning [15]; Islam et al. further constructed the UFO-120 dataset and proposed a joint framework for simultaneous enhancement and super-resolution [16]. AMPCNet, proposed by Zhang et al., adaptively focuses on key regions of underwater targets through an attention-guided multi-path cross CNN [17]; Ren et al. proposed URSCT, fusing an enhanced Swin-Convs Transformer with a convolutional network to achieve collaborative optimisation of underwater image enhancement and super-resolution [18]; DeepWaveNet, proposed by Sharma et al., explicitly models the attenuation laws of light of different wavelengths in water and achieves excellent results in colour restoration [19]; Chen et al. proposed RDLN, which through multi-scale feature extraction combined with collaborative learning of long- and short-range dependencies effectively solves the problem of coexisting local distortion and global blur in underwater images [20]; Chen et al. proposed the Progressive Attention Learning (PAL) method, which restores underwater image detail in stages through a progressively refined attention strategy [21]; Cherian et al.
168: proposed the AlphaSRGAN method, achieving a good balance between detail restoration and perceptual quality [22]; Pramanick et al.
169: proposed a multi-resolution, multi-scale attention underwater image restoration method, comprehensively exploiting features at different scales to achieve detail reconstruction [23]. Related research in 2026 further combines enhancement, saliency modelling and super-resolution reconstruction: DeFu-UIESR adopts a saliency-guided dual-branch decoupled fusion framework to handle underwater image enhancement and super-resolution simultaneously; the lightweight frequency-domain Transformer network proposed by Wu et al. improves reconstruction efficiency and detail fidelity from the perspective of frequency modelling [24][25]. In terms of frequency-domain modelling, Dharejo et al. proposed SwinWave-SR, combining the Swin Transformer with the wavelet transform to achieve lightweight, high-quality underwater image super-resolution reconstruction on the basis of multi-scale frequency decomposition [26]; the wavelet super-resolution method proposed by Chen et al. introduces wavelet-domain information into underwater image reconstruction, further enriching the technical approach to frequency-domain modelling [27]; Wang et al. introduced spatial-frequency mutual learning into super-resolution networks, significantly improving the reconstruction capability for fine textures through the coordinated combination of frequency-domain global modelling and spatial-domain local modelling, providing important reference for the frequency-domain/spatial-domain coupled design of this thesis [28]. From the perspective of image decomposition, Zhou et al. proposed a texture-structure-aware image decomposition neural network model, revealing the theoretical basis that an image can be expressed as the sum of a texture layer and a structure layer, which lays the theoretical foundation for the design of the texture-structure joint loss in this thesis [29]. In terms of Transformer architectures, the Swin Transformer proposed by Liu et al. achieves global information perception at linear computational complexity through a local-window attention mechanism, and has become one of the most important backbone networks for current visual super-resolution [30]; Liang et al. introduced the Swin Transformer into the image super-resolution framework to propose SwinIR, achieving then-leading reconstruction performance in general scenes [31]. In terms of underwater Transformer methods, Wang et al. proposed a frequency-domain Transformer-based underwater image restoration method [32]; Shen et al. proposed UDAformer, performing underwater image enhancement based on a dual-attention Transformer [33]; Peng et al. proposed a U-shaped Transformer applied to the underwater image enhancement task [34] - all of which provide new ideas for underwater image quality improvement from the perspective of global modelling.
170: In summary, existing super-resolution methods have made significant progress in general scenes, but the exploitation of frequency-domain priors for underwater images remains insufficient, and the decoupled supervision of the image texture layer and structure layer by loss functions is still imperfect. It is precisely these shortcomings that this thesis addresses by proposing the FSCIN network, which systematically improves underwater image super-resolution reconstruction quality along two dimensions - frequency-domain/spatial-domain collaborative modelling and a texture-structure joint loss - with its output serving directly as the high-quality input to the subsequent object detection module.
171: 1.2.2 Research Status of Underwater Image Object Detection
172: Object detection is a core task in the field of computer vision, aiming to simultaneously accomplish the localisation and classification of targets in an image, and is in strong demand in applications such as underwater robot navigation, marine biological monitoring and underwater security. Current deep-learning object detection methods can be divided, according to their processing flow, into two major categories: two-stage detection and one-stage detection. In terms of two-stage detection methods, R-CNN, proposed by Girshick et al., generates candidate regions through selective search and uses a convolutional neural network to extract features, pioneering research into deep learning in the field of object detection [35]; Girshick further proposed Fast R-CNN, which significantly improved detection efficiency by sharing
174: convolutional feature maps [36]; Ren et al. proposed Faster R-CNN, which fuses a region proposal network (RPN)
175: with the detection network end-to-end and made important advances in both accuracy and speed, becoming a milestone in two-stage detection methods [37]. The feature pyramid network (FPN) proposed by Lin et al. achieves multi-scale feature fusion through a top-down semantic path and a bottom-up positional information path, effectively improving detection capability for targets of different sizes, and has been widely integrated into various detection frameworks [38]. In underwater scenes, Jia et al. proposed an underwater object detection method based on an improved EfficientDet and compared multiple classes of detection model on datasets such as URPC, verifying the effectiveness of feature enhancement and multi-scale fusion for target recognition in complex underwater scenes, laying a foundation for subsequent underwater detection research [39].
176: In terms of one-stage detection methods, YOLO (You Only Look Once), proposed by Redmon et al., models object detection as a regression problem solved in a single forward inference pass, outputting target position and category simultaneously in an end-to-end manner and achieving a breakthrough improvement in detection speed [40]. Thereafter the YOLO series continued to iterate and evolve: Bochkovskiy et al. proposed YOLOv4, introducing the CSP cross-stage partial connection network and a variety of data augmentation strategies [41]; Jocher et al. proposed YOLOv5, improving engineering deployability through a lightweight design [42]; YOLOv8, proposed by Jocher et al., adopts the C2f module in place of the original C3 module, introduces a decoupled detection head and optimises the PAN-FPN structure, achieving comprehensive performance that balances accuracy and efficiency on general object detection tasks, and has been widely applied in various engineering scenarios [43]. Among one-stage methods developed in parallel with YOLO, SSD, proposed by Liu et al., achieves better multi-scale target coverage through dense prediction on multi-scale feature maps [44]; RetinaNet, proposed by Lin et al., introduced Focal Loss to solve the problem of extreme positive/negative sample imbalance in one-stage detection, substantially improving detection accuracy [45]. In terms of feature enhancement and attention mechanisms, SENet, proposed by Hu et al., applies adaptive weights to different semantic channels through a channel attention mechanism [46]; CBAM, proposed by Woo et al., cascades spatial attention on top of channel attention, further guiding the network to focus on salient target regions and effectively suppressing interference from underwater background clutter [47]. Recent underwater object detection research has further centred on small targets, complex backgrounds and multi-scale feature fusion: YOLO-Starfish improves starfish target detection accuracy through an improved YOLOv8, while YOLO-MFD introduces a dynamic detection head and a multi-scale feature fusion strategy for complex underwater environments, providing reference for the subsequent object detection improvements in this thesis [48][49].
177: In terms of Transformer-based detection methods, the Vision Transformer (ViT) proposed by Dosovitskiy et al. divides an image into a sequence of patches which are fed into a Transformer encoder, establishing long-range dependencies between pixels through a global self-attention mechanism and providing stronger global context modelling capability for visual detection tasks [50]; Carion et al. proposed DETR based on the Transformer, achieving object detection in an end-to-end manner and eliminating complex post-processing steps such as traditional anchor-box design and non-maximum suppression [51]; Zhu et al. further proposed Deformable DETR, introducing a deformable attention mechanism to solve the problems of slow convergence and weak small-target detection [52]. However, the quadratic computational complexity of the Transformer still poses challenges for deployment on real-time embedded underwater platforms. Addressing this limitation, state space models (SSMs) represented by Mamba provide a new technical path: the structured state space model (S4) proposed by Gu et al. demonstrated the feasibility of SSMs capturing long-range dependencies in long-sequence modelling with
179: linear complexity [53]; Mamba, proposed by Gu and Dao, introduces a selective scan mechanism and, through
180: an input-adaptive parameter update strategy, achieves more efficient global information modelling than the standard Transformer, replacing the Transformer's O(L2) with linear O(L) complexity and providing an effective modelling tool for the global blur problem in underwater images caused by scattering [54].
181: In summary, existing underwater object detection methods have achieved good results in general scenes, but clear limitations remain in three areas: fine-grained perception of small targets, global dependency modelling, and adaptive multi-scale feature fusion. It is particularly worth noting that the low contrast and texture degradation inherent in underwater images directly weaken the feature extraction capability of detection networks, and improving the detection model structure alone cannot fundamentally solve the problem of insufficient input image quality. Therefore, this thesis unifies the two tasks of super-resolution enhancement and object detection within the complete processing framework "original image -> sharpening -> clear image -> object detection -> detection result", collaboratively improving the overall performance of the underwater object detection system along the two dimensions of input quality and model capability.
183: Addressing problems such as underwater image quality degradation and insufficient object detection accuracy, this thesis conducts research centred on underwater image super-resolution reconstruction and object detection, and constructs an underwater visual perception framework with the complete processing chain "original underwater image -> super-resolution sharpening -> high-quality clear image -> object detection -> detection result", as shown in Figure 1.3. The core logic of this framework is: in the first stage, super-resolution enhancement compensates for the effects of underwater degradation at the image-quality level; in the second stage, object detection is performed on the basis of the high-quality image. The cascaded collaboration of the two improves overall system performance. The specific research route is shown in Figure 1.3 below.
185: First, addressing degradation problems present in underwater images such as insufficient contrast, blurred detail and colour deviation, the Frequency-domain-Spatial-domain Coupled Inference Network (FSCIN) is proposed, and a spatial-frequency awareness module (SFAM) is designed that combines the fast Fourier transform with
187: the spatial-domain encoding of the Swin Transformer, achieving deep fusion of frequency-domain global priors and spatial-domain local features; at the same time,
188: a texture-structure joint loss function is introduced which applies targeted constraints to the image texture layer and structure layer separately, significantly improving the perceptual quality and detail fidelity of underwater images. The high-quality clear images output by FSCIN serve directly as the input to the object detection stage, forming the front-end processing module of the overall framework.
189: Second, on the basis of the high-quality clear images output by FSCIN, targeted improvements are made to the YOLOv8 model: a fine-grained feature extraction module (FFEM) is designed to replace the original C2f module. This module is built collaboratively from three sub-modules - the channel-spatial adaptive enhancement module, the Mamba-based global perception module, and the multi-scale cross-attention fusion module - which respectively improve the detection capability for underwater targets along three dimensions: local fine-grained perception, global long-range dependency modelling, and dynamic cross-scale feature fusion.
190: Finally, through systematic experiments on the public datasets USR-248, UFO-120 (super-resolution reconstruction) and URPC2021 (object detection), the effectiveness of FSCIN and of the improved YOLOv8 is verified respectively, and the actual improvement effect of super-resolution pre-processing on object detection performance is analysed, in order to quantitatively evaluate the overall benefit of the "enhancement-detection" cascaded framework.
192: This thesis conducts research centred mainly on underwater image super-resolution reconstruction and object detection methods; the structure of the thesis is arranged as shown in Figure 1.4.
195: Chapter 1 is the introduction. It presents the research background and significance, and reviews the research status at home and abroad in the two
196: directions of underwater image super-resolution reconstruction and object detection, clarifies the overall technical thinking behind this thesis's "enhancement-detection" cascaded framework, and sets out the main research content and organisational structure of the thesis.
197: Chapter 2 covers related theoretical foundations. It introduces the underwater image degradation model, the principles of super-resolution reconstruction, and the core deep learning modules (including convolutional neural networks, the Transformer model, the Mamba model and object detection theory), providing theoretical support for subsequent chapters.
198: Chapter 3 is the first-stage work of this thesis's "enhancement-detection" framework. It proposes an underwater image super-resolution reconstruction method based on the Frequency-domain-Spatial-domain Coupled Inference Network (FSCIN), and details the network structure design, the core SFAM module and the texture-structure joint loss. The high-quality clear images output by this chapter serve directly as the input to the object detection of Chapter 4, forming the front-end processing module of the overall framework.
199: Chapter 4 is the second-stage work of this thesis's "enhancement-detection" framework. On the basis of the super-resolution enhanced images of Chapter 3, it proposes an underwater object detection method based on an improved YOLOv8, and details the design and experimental verification of the FFEM module. Chapter 5 summarises the work of the whole thesis, analyses the collaborative role of the two core modules within the complete "enhancement-detection" framework, and offers an outlook on future research directions.
